quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Shell, Paths, and Navigation
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand shells, path types, and basic navigation before file operations and pipes.

questions.prompt: What is a shell in beginner terms?

options.text: A graphical image editor bundled with every website
A program that interprets the commands you type in a terminal
A type of hard disk partition only
A CSS framework for servers

questions.explanation: The shell reads your commands and runs programs accordingly.

wrongExplanations.c: Partitions are storage concepts, not the shell itself.
wrongExplanations.d: CSS frameworks are unrelated to the terminal shell.

options.text: docs/intro.md
/var/log/syslog
../README.md
./src

questions.explanation: Absolute paths start from the filesystem root `/`.

wrongExplanations.a: That relative path depends on the current directory.
wrongExplanations.c: `..` makes this relative to the parent of the current directory.
wrongExplanations.d: `./` explicitly means relative to the current directory.

options.text: The password database for all users
Your current working directory
All environment variables permanently deleted
The contents of every file on disk

questions.explanation: pwd prints the present working directory—where relative paths start from.

wrongExplanations.a: pwd is not a password tool.
wrongExplanations.c: pwd does not delete environment variables.
wrongExplanations.d: Listing file contents is what tools like cat/less do for specific files.

options.text: Deletes the parent directory
Moves you into the parent of the current directory
Creates a new root filesystem
Clears the terminal history only

questions.explanation: `..` means the parent directory; cd changes into it.

wrongExplanations.a: cd navigates; it does not delete directories.
wrongExplanations.d: History clearing is a different action.

questions.prompt: Why is ls -la useful for beginners?

options.text: It formats disks automatically
It lists details and includes hidden dotfiles that ordinary ls may omit
It emails the file list to your team
It disables permissions on all files

questions.explanation: `-l` adds details and `-a` shows hidden entries such as `.env` and `.git`.

wrongExplanations.c: It prints to the terminal; it does not email.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Files, Text, Permissions, and Pipes
quizzes.intro: Test file operations, inspection tools, chmod mindset, and command composition.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between > and >> when redirecting output?

options.text: They are identical in all shells
> overwrites a file; >> appends to a file
> appends; >> always deletes the directory tree
>> only works with images

questions.explanation: Single > truncates/overwrites; >> adds to the end.

wrongExplanations.a: Their overwrite versus append behavior differs importantly.
wrongExplanations.c: That reverses the meanings and invents directory deletion.
wrongExplanations.d: Redirection works with text streams generally, not only images.

options.text: Deletes the left-hand command from disk
Sends the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next
Creates a graphical window for every command
Converts files into PDFs automatically

questions.explanation: Pipes compose tools by connecting output to input.

wrongExplanations.c: Pipes are text-stream connections, not GUI spawners.
wrongExplanations.d: PDF conversion is unrelated to the pipe operator itself.

questions.prompt: Why is rm -r dangerous if used carelessly?

options.text: Because it only prints filenames and never deletes
Because recursive deletion can remove entire directory trees and often has no Trash undo
Because it installs packages as root automatically
Because it renames files to safer backups by default

questions.explanation: Recursive remove can wipe large trees quickly with little recovery on many systems.

wrongExplanations.a: rm deletes; it is not a dry-run printer by default.
wrongExplanations.c: Package installs are a different class of commands.

questions.prompt: What is a beginner-friendly interpretation of chmod u+x script.sh?

options.text: Delete the script for the user
Add execute permission for the file owner so it can be run as a program
Upload the script to the cloud
Encrypt the script with a password prompt every time

questions.explanation: `u+x` grants the owner execute permission, commonly needed for shell scripts.

wrongExplanations.a: chmod changes permissions; it does not delete the file.
wrongExplanations.c: chmod is local permission change, not upload.

questions.prompt: Which tool is commonly used to search for matching lines inside files?

options.text: grep
mkdir
pwd
cd

questions.explanation: grep filters lines that match a pattern; -R can search directories recursively.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Processes, Environment, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply command-line judgment to processes, PATH, sudo, and safe habits.

questions.prompt: What does Ctrl+C typically do to a foreground terminal process?

options.text: Copies the entire hard drive
Interrupts the process
Increases process priority permanently
Formats /home

questions.explanation: Ctrl+C sends an interrupt signal to the foreground process in typical terminal setups.

options.text: Listing directories the shell searches to find executable commands
Storing only image assets for websites
Disabling all permissions
Replacing the need for file names

questions.explanation: When you type a command, the shell looks through PATH entries to locate the program.

wrongExplanations.b: PATH is about executables, not website images.
wrongExplanations.d: You still use command and file names.

questions.prompt: What is the safest beginner attitude toward sudo?

options.text: Use it on every command so nothing ever fails
Use it only when you understand why elevated privileges are required
Never learn what it does
Assume it undeletes any rm mistake automatically

questions.explanation: Elevation is powerful; understanding necessity reduces accidental system damage.

wrongExplanations.a: Blanket sudo increases risk and hides permission problems.
wrongExplanations.c: You should understand it precisely because it is powerful.
wrongExplanations.d: sudo does not provide a universal undelete for rm.

questions.prompt: Before running a destructive command, which check is most essential?

options.text: Confirming your working directory and exact target path
Closing your eyes and typing faster
Disabling all backups first
Piping the command into rm -rf / without reading it

questions.explanation: Knowing where you are and what path you target prevents many catastrophic mistakes.

wrongExplanations.c: Backups are protection, not something to disable first.
wrongExplanations.d: That is an example of extreme unsafe behavior.

questions.prompt: What does kill PID typically attempt?

options.text: To create a new user account named PID
To send a signal to a process, by default requesting termination
To print the manual for every package
To change file ownership recursively

questions.explanation: kill signals a process; the default signal asks it to terminate.

wrongExplanations.a: User creation is a different administrative task.
wrongExplanations.c: Manual pages are read with man, not kill.

questions.prompt: A command fails with “No such file or directory,” but you are sure the file exists somewhere. What should you verify first?

options.text: That relative vs absolute path and current directory (`pwd`) match your assumption
That the internet is offline forever
That all man pages are deleted
That pipes are illegal on your system

questions.explanation: Most beginner path errors come from being in the wrong directory or using the wrong path form.

wrongExplanations.b: Network state is usually unrelated to local path resolution.
wrongExplanations.c: Man pages are not the first suspect.
wrongExplanations.d: Pipes remain valid in normal shells.
